essays.question: Some argue that the internet is the main reason for social problems. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Cyberbullying, online scams, false news and loneliness are regularly blamed on the internet, and some argue that it is the main reason for social problems. I disagree to a large extent, since the internet magnifies social problems but rarely creates them, and its benefits are also considerable.

To begin with, the internet magnifies social problems but rarely creates them. Bullying, misinformation and isolation existed before, and the internet makes them faster and more visible, while the underlying causes are poverty, family breakdown and weak education. A false rumour about a neighbour, for example, once spread slowly by gossip but can now reach thousands in minutes. This amplification is serious, since victims may face abuse at any hour, but the roots of the behaviour lie in human attitudes and social conditions, not in cables and servers. Crime, inequality, addiction and discrimination all existed long before the internet and still exist in places where few people are online.

Furthermore, the internet also helps to solve social problems. It allows isolated people to find communities, helps victims to report abuse, gives access to education and health information, and enables campaigns for change. During crises, such as pandemics, online tools kept schools, businesses and families connected. However, it would be wrong to ignore real harm. Algorithms that reward outrage can increase division, and heavy use may affect the wellbeing of some young people. Governments and platforms should therefore regulate harmful content, protect children and teach digital skills, while also tackling the social conditions that make people vulnerable. Without addressing these deeper causes, restricting the internet alone would solve little.

In conclusion, the internet is not the main reason for social problems, because it mostly amplifies difficulties that have other causes, although it can aggravate them and needs sensible regulation.

essays.question: Some people believe that science and technology improve people’s lives. Others think they cause problems. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
From antibiotics to smartphones, science and technology have changed almost every part of daily life, and opinions are divided as to whether they improve people's lives or cause problems. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that science and technology have raised living standards in health, communication and convenience. Vaccines and medical devices save lives, the internet and mobile networks connect people instantly, and machines make work and housework faster. A villager who consults a city doctor by video, for example, receives expert advice without travelling for hours. Advances in agriculture, transport and energy have reduced hunger and poverty and allowed people to live longer and more comfortable lives. Knowledge is more accessible than ever, which helps education and personal development, and technology creates new industries and careers.

On the other hand, critics point out that technology also causes problems. Automation can destroy jobs, factories and vehicles pollute the environment, weapons are more destructive, and personal data are collected on a huge scale, which threatens privacy. Many people feel overwhelmed by screens, notifications and constant connection, and it can reduce attention and face-to-face contact. Dependence on complex systems makes societies vulnerable when they fail, as in power cuts or cyber-attacks. Some argue that technology has also widened the gap between rich and poor, since the benefits are not shared equally.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that science and technology improve life overall, but their harmful effects must be managed through regulation, education and responsible use.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on technology? Use examples.

versions.text:
Technology now shapes every industry, from farming to finance, and many governments see it as the key to prosperity. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on technology: a stronger economy and better public services.

First and foremost, a country that invests in technology becomes more productive and competitive. High-tech industries create well-paid jobs and exports, and digital tools help every business, from small shops to large factories, to work faster and reach more customers. A country that allows citizens to file taxes and vote online, for example, saves time and money for both government and residents. Technology also attracts investment and talented people, and it helps countries to create new products instead of competing only on low costs. Nations such as South Korea and Singapore have built prosperity by combining education with strong technology sectors.

In addition, technology improves public services and quality of life. Digital records allow hospitals to share information safely, online services reduce queues and paperwork, and data helps cities to manage traffic, energy and waste. A villager who consults a city doctor by video, for example, receives expert advice without travelling for hours. Farmers use sensors and satellite information to grow more with fewer resources, and online education reaches students who live far from good schools. Although technology requires investment, training and protection against misuse, such as privacy violations, a country that plans carefully can enjoy long-term gains. Governments should also ensure that everyone has access, so that the benefits are shared.

To sum up, focusing on technology brings clear benefits to a country, above all a stronger economy and better public services. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Many people think that automation has improved people’s lives. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Robots weld cars, software sorts parcels and self-service machines process payments, and many people think that automation has improved people's lives. I agree with this view, since automation removes dangerous and repetitive work and makes goods cheaper, although it also creates difficulties that need to be managed.

To begin with, automation removes dangerous and repetitive work and makes goods cheaper. Machines handle heavy lifting, hazardous chemicals and repetitive assembly, raising productivity and lowering prices. A robot that welds car parts, for example, protects workers from fumes and produces more consistent results. Factories that use automation have fewer accidents, and products such as cars, phones and food are more affordable than they would otherwise be. Automation in offices removes tedious tasks like data entry, so that people can concentrate on more interesting work involving judgement and creativity. Hospitals use automated systems to deliver supplies and process test results, which frees nurses to care for patients.

Furthermore, automation has created new jobs in design, maintenance, programming and services, and it has allowed people to enjoy shorter working hours and more leisure than previous generations. However, workers whose jobs disappear need retraining and support, and automation may widen inequality if the gains go only to owners of machines. Towns that depended on a single factory can suffer badly. Governments and employers should therefore invest in education and retraining, provide support for those who lose jobs and ensure that the benefits are shared through fair taxation and wages. When managed well, automation improves living standards for most people.

In conclusion, I agree that automation has improved people's lives, because it makes work safer and goods cheaper, provided that those who lose out are supported.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on science and research? Use examples.

versions.text:
Research laboratories, universities and observatories rarely make headlines, but their discoveries shape medicine, industry and daily life, and many countries invest heavily in them. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on science and research: economic growth and solutions to national and global problems.

First and foremost, a country that invests in science and research becomes more productive and competitive. High-tech industries create well-paid jobs and exports, and the knowledge produced by universities leads to new products and companies. Many of today's industries, from the internet to biotechnology, grew from basic research that had no immediate commercial aim. A country that supports research can also attract talented scientists and investors from abroad, and benefit from patents and spin-off businesses. South Korea and Germany show how sustained investment in research and engineering can support strong, innovative economies.

In addition, science provides the knowledge to solve major problems. Basic research produces medicines, vaccines, materials and clean energy technologies, and scientists help governments to deal with disease, climate change and food shortages. Research also trains highly skilled people who work in industry, teaching and government, and it raises the general level of education. During a pandemic, for example, a country with strong research capacity can develop tests and vaccines more quickly and protect its population. Although research is expensive, uncertain and slow to deliver, and not every project succeeds, the long-term returns have been very large. Governments should therefore give researchers stable funding and freedom to pursue ideas.

To sum up, focusing on science and research brings clear benefits to a country, above all economic growth and the ability to solve major problems. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Many people think that smartphone use has improved people’s lives. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
In little more than a decade, smartphones have become part of daily life for billions of people, and many think that smartphone use has improved people's lives. I agree with this view, since smartphones put communication, information and services in everyone's pocket, although they have costs that users should manage.

To begin with, smartphones put communication, information and services in everyone's pocket. People can contact family, find directions, bank, shop and call for help from one device. A traveller who is lost in an unfamiliar city, for example, can find the way, translate a menu and call a taxi with one phone. Students can access encyclopaedias and lessons, workers can answer messages while away from the office, and farmers in remote villages can check weather forecasts and market prices. In emergencies, a phone can call for help or share location, which has saved many lives. Camera, maps, music and payments in one device would have required many gadgets in the past.

Furthermore, smartphones have widened access to services for people who were previously excluded, such as mobile banking in places without branches and health advice in remote areas. However, there are real costs. Constant notifications and social media can be addictive and distracting, sleep and concentration may suffer, and personal data may be collected and misused. Children and teenagers are especially vulnerable to pressure and bullying. Users can reduce these risks by setting limits, turning off notifications, protecting privacy and putting the phone aside during meals and before bed. The value of a smartphone therefore depends on how sensibly it is used.

In conclusion, I agree that smartphones have improved people's lives, because they provide convenience, information and safety, provided that people use them in moderation.

essays.question: Some people believe that space exploration is essential for human progress. Others think it is a waste of resources. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Rockets, probes and space telescopes cost enormous sums, and opinions differ on whether space exploration is essential for human progress or a waste of resources. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that space exploration drives technology and knowledge that benefit people on Earth. Missions require advances in materials, medicine, communications and computing that later spread to everyday use, and satellites provide weather forecasts, navigation and climate data. A farmer who receives a satellite weather forecast, for example, can decide when to plant and avoid losing a crop. Exploration also inspires young people to study science and engineering, and it deepens our understanding of the origin of the universe. Some experts add that learning about other planets helps us to understand and protect our own, and that a future in which humans live beyond Earth may become a necessary insurance.

On the other hand, critics point out that space programmes cost enormous sums that could address urgent problems on Earth. Missions run to billions, with uncertain returns, while hospitals, schools and housing lack funds, and failures waste money and sometimes lives. The sum spent on a single mission, for example, could equip dozens of hospitals in poorer regions. Critics also argue that private firms may now fund exploration, so that governments need not use taxes for it, and that many benefits of space technology could be obtained more cheaply through other research.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that space exploration is worthwhile in moderate amounts, because it produces practical returns, but governments should never allow it to take priority over basic needs.

essays.question: How far do you think virtual reality will change entertainment in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Headsets that place users inside a game or a concert are already on sale, and many people expect virtual reality to transform entertainment within twenty years. I believe that it will change some forms of entertainment greatly, although it is unlikely to replace traditional ones.

To begin with, virtual reality will change entertainment in gaming and live events. Headsets offer immersion that screens cannot, so that players feel inside the story and audiences feel present at events they cannot attend. A fan who cannot travel, for example, can watch a concert in virtual reality as if standing near the stage. As headsets become lighter and cheaper, theme parks, museums and cinemas will offer virtual experiences, and new types of storytelling will appear, in which viewers move around inside a scene. Social platforms in which friends meet as avatars will also grow, since people enjoy shared experiences.

However, virtual reality will probably not replace traditional forms. Cost, motion sickness and limited content keep many people away, and wearing a headset for long periods is tiring and isolating. People still enjoy sharing cinemas, concerts and television with others, and a large proportion of audiences prefer to sit back and relax instead of moving and interacting. History offers examples: television did not destroy cinema, and streaming did not end live music. Virtual reality will therefore be an important addition, not a complete replacement, and it will probably dominate only in gaming.

In conclusion, virtual reality will change entertainment to a considerable extent over the next twenty years, but traditional forms will survive alongside it.

essays.question: Some believe that genetically modified food is beneficial. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Genetically modified crops are grown in many countries and banned in others, and some believe that genetically modified food is beneficial. I largely agree, since modified crops can raise yields and improve nutrition, although careful regulation and honest labelling are essential.

To begin with, genetically modified food can be beneficial when it is regulated and tested. Modified crops can resist disease, survive drought and carry extra nutrients, which raises yields and reduces chemical use. A rice variety enriched with vitamin A, for example, could help to prevent blindness in children whose diet lacks it. Farmers who plant pest-resistant varieties use fewer pesticides, which protects both their health and the environment, and crops that tolerate poor soil or dry weather can provide food where traditional varieties fail. With the global population rising and climate change affecting harvests, technologies that increase output without clearing more land have clear value.

Furthermore, scientific reviews by major health organisations have found that approved modified foods are as safe to eat as their conventional equivalents. However, concerns should not be dismissed. Some people worry about long-term effects on health and ecosystems, the spread of modified genes to wild plants, and the control of seeds by a few large companies. Public trust is important, so governments should require independent testing, publish the results and label modified products so that consumers can choose. Support for small farmers and public research, instead of dependence on private companies, would also help to share the benefits. Where safety and fairness are ensured, modified food can be a valuable tool in the fight against hunger.

In conclusion, I largely agree that genetically modified food is beneficial, because it can increase food supplies and nutrition, provided that it is tested and regulated carefully.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on technological innovation? Use examples.

versions.text:
New inventions, from electric cars to artificial intelligence, appear every year, and governments are keen to encourage innovation. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on technological innovation: new industries and jobs, and improved efficiency and quality of life.

First and foremost, technological innovation creates new industries, jobs and exports. A company that develops a better battery or a new medical device can grow into a major employer, and clusters of such firms attract suppliers, researchers and investors. A country that becomes known for efficient batteries, for instance, can sell them to many others. Innovative countries earn a reputation that attracts talented workers and international investment, and they are less dependent on exporting raw materials or low-cost goods. Start-up companies also create competition, which pushes older firms to improve. Societies that encourage experimentation tend to adapt more quickly to economic change.

In addition, innovation improves efficiency and quality of life. New technologies in health, transport and energy reduce costs, save time and cut pollution. A farm that switches from flooding its fields to drip irrigation, for example, can grow the same crop with far less water. Innovations such as online banking, ride-sharing and telemedicine make services cheaper and more convenient, and clean technology helps countries to meet environmental goals. Although innovation brings risks, such as job changes and ethical questions, and not every idea succeeds, governments can reduce these through education, retraining, and sensible regulation. A society that invests in innovation prepares itself for the challenges of the future.

To sum up, technological innovation brings clear benefits to a country, above all new industries and jobs and a better quality of life. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: How can governments address the digital divide? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Increasingly, banking, education, job applications and government services are available mainly online, yet millions of people still cannot take part, and the gap between those with and without digital access is known as the digital divide. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on reducing the cost of access and on improving infrastructure and skills.

To begin with, governments should make devices and connections affordable. The digital divide comes from cost, poor infrastructure and lack of skills, and each cause needs its own remedy. Families on low incomes cannot afford devices or data, so subsidies for basic computers, low-cost data plans and free public wifi can help them. A student without internet at home, for example, can do homework at a library that offers free computers and wifi. Schools can lend tablets and laptops to pupils who do not have them, and companies can be encouraged to offer social tariffs to low-income households.

In addition, authorities should improve infrastructure and teach skills. Rural areas need cables and signals, and public investment can reach places that private firms find unprofitable. Training programmes for older people, jobseekers and migrants, delivered in libraries, community centres and workplaces, teach them how to use online services safely. Equally important, government services should remain available through phone or in person for those who cannot go online, so that nobody is shut out while the gap is being closed. Digital skills should also be taught in schools from an early age. Reducing the gap is an investment, since people who are online can find work, study and access public services at lower cost.

In conclusion, making access affordable and improving infrastructure and skills offer the most realistic way of addressing the digital divide.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on research or on public services? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Governments must choose between funding scientific research and funding services such as health, education and welfare, and opinions differ on which should come first. This essay will discuss both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, those who favour public services argue that they meet urgent needs. Hospitals, schools and welfare protect health, give children an education and support the vulnerable, and these needs cannot wait. A family that cannot see a doctor, for example, suffers immediately, whereas the results of research may take decades to appear. Services also create a healthy and educated population, which is the basis of a strong economy. Many people feel that it is unfair to spend public money on laboratories while basic needs remain unmet, and voters generally expect governments to serve them directly.

On the other hand, supporters of research argue that it is a long-term investment. Research produces discoveries, jobs and growth that pay for future services. Years of earlier research, for example, allowed scientists to develop vaccines quickly when a new virus appeared. Private companies often avoid basic research because the returns are uncertain, so that only governments can fund it, and countries that cut research risk falling behind in the technology and medicine of the future. Research also trains skilled workers, who add to national income and improve public services themselves.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that governments should fund services first, since they meet urgent needs, but keep research as a protected long-term investment, because a balanced budget serves both present and future needs.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for digital privacy, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Every search, purchase and message leaves a trace, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for digital privacy or whether society and government should take action. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that individuals can do a great deal to protect their own information. Users can check the privacy settings of apps, use strong and different passwords, think before sharing personal details and avoid suspicious links. A user who reviews the privacy settings of an app, for example, can stop it from sharing her location with advertisers. People who understand how their data are collected can choose services that respect privacy and refuse those that do not, and this encourages companies to compete on protection. Since no law can protect someone who posts private details publicly, personal care is the first line of defence.

On the other hand, advocates of action by society and government point out that most individuals cannot control how their data are used. Digital privacy needs both careful users and strong protection from companies and governments. Terms and conditions are long and complicated, and companies collect, store and sell vast quantities of data in ways that users cannot see. Only laws and standards can limit what organisations collect, require them to secure data, give citizens the right to see and delete their information and impose penalties for abuse. Regulators can also act against data breaches that affect millions of people at once, which no individual could prevent.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that the most effective approach combines official leadership with personal action, since governments must set clear rules for organisations while individuals take sensible precautions.

essays.question: How far do you think wearable technology will change personal health monitoring in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Smartwatches and fitness bands already count steps and measure heart rate, and many people expect wearable technology to change personal health monitoring greatly within twenty years. I believe that it will change it to a large extent, although it will support doctors and not replace them.

To begin with, wearable devices will make health monitoring continuous and personal. Sensors track heart rate, sleep and activity all day and can alert users and doctors early. A smartwatch that notices an irregular heartbeat, for example, can advise its owner to see a doctor before a serious problem develops. In the future, devices will probably measure blood sugar, blood pressure and oxygen without needles, and artificial intelligence will interpret the data. This is especially valuable for people with chronic conditions and for older adults, who can be monitored at home and treated before they need hospital care. It will also lower costs for health systems, because prevention is cheaper than treatment.

However, accuracy and privacy limit the role of wearables. Readings are sometimes unreliable, can cause needless anxiety and produce data that companies may misuse or sell to insurers. Wearables are also expensive, so that poorer people may benefit less, and many users abandon a device after a few months. Medical decisions still need trained professionals who can examine patients and consider the whole picture. Wearables will therefore support, not replace, medical care.

In conclusion, wearable technology will transform personal health monitoring to a large extent over the next twenty years, but concerns about accuracy, privacy and fairness must be addressed.

essays.question: How far do you think blockchain technology will affect banking in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Blockchain began as the technology behind digital currencies, and many people expect it to affect banking greatly within twenty years. I believe that it will change parts of banking, mainly payments and record keeping, although it will not remove banks.

To begin with, blockchain will change the way money moves and is recorded. Shared ledgers allow faster and cheaper transfers across borders and reduce the need for intermediaries. A worker abroad who sends money home, for example, may pay high fees and wait days, whereas a blockchain transfer can arrive within minutes at lower cost. Transactions are recorded in a way that is difficult to alter, which increases transparency and may reduce fraud. Smart contracts can carry out agreements automatically, for instance by releasing a payment when goods are delivered, and banks can use them to lower administration costs. Several major banks and central banks are already testing digital currencies and settlement systems.

However, change will be significant but gradual. Regulation is still uncertain, prices of some digital assets swing wildly, and security failures at exchanges have caused large losses. Many customers value the trust, insurance and customer service that established banks provide, and governments want control over their money supply. Blockchain also consumes energy in some forms. For these reasons, banks are likely to adopt the technology rather than disappear, using it to improve payments and record keeping behind the scenes.

In conclusion, blockchain will affect banking to a considerable extent over the next twenty years, particularly in international payments, but the change will be gradual and led mainly by existing institutions.

essays.question: Many feel that photo editing apps create unrealistic beauty standards. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
With a single tap, an app can smooth skin, reshape a jaw or brighten eyes, and many feel that photo editing apps create unrealistic beauty standards. I agree with this view, since edited images make unrealistic appearances look normal, although awareness and rules can reduce the harm.

To begin with, photo editing apps make unrealistic images look normal. Filters smooth skin, change shapes and brighten features so well that edited faces seem real, and young people who compare themselves with them may feel dissatisfied with their own bodies. A teenager who edits every selfie to make her skin flawless, for example, may start to believe that her real face is unattractive. Because many images on social media are edited, often without any label, users see a stream of apparently perfect people and may assume that this is the standard. Studies have linked heavy use of such images to anxiety about appearance, low self-esteem and, in some cases, eating disorders and cosmetic surgery requests.

Furthermore, the pressure affects people of all ages and genders, and it can be reinforced by advertising and celebrities who use the same tools. Editing also changes the ideal over time, so that what is considered beautiful becomes increasingly narrow. However, the apps themselves are not entirely to blame, since people have long manipulated images with make-up and airbrushing. Some users employ filters for fun or creativity, and many people are aware that images are edited. Education about editing in schools, clear labels on altered advertising images and platforms that reduce the promotion of heavy filters can limit the damage. Encouraging people to value diversity and natural appearances also helps.

In conclusion, I agree that photo editing apps create unrealistic beauty standards, because they make edited looks seem normal, though education and honest labelling can reduce the harm.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using surveillance cameras in public places.

versions.text:
Cameras now watch streets, shops, stations and car parks in most cities, and the question is whether their advantages outweigh their disadvantages. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using surveillance cameras in public places before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, surveillance cameras can deter crime and provide evidence. Visible cameras discourage theft and vandalism, and recordings help police to identify and convict offenders. A camera that covers a poorly lit car park, for example, helps police to identify thieves and makes drivers feel safer. Footage can also help to find missing people, to understand accidents and to protect staff from abuse, and the public often feel more secure in monitored areas. In serious cases, such as terrorist attacks, camera evidence has been vital in tracing suspects quickly. Cameras in transport systems also help to manage crowds and respond to emergencies.

On the negative side, cameras raise privacy and cost concerns. They record innocent people as well as offenders, and combined with facial recognition they can track individuals' movements. Footage can be misused or leaked, and people who feel constantly watched may be less free to act naturally. Cameras are expensive to buy, maintain and monitor, and evidence on their effect is mixed: they may only move crime to areas without cameras, and they do little to prevent crimes of passion. Misidentification by software has led to wrongful accusations. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced if cameras are placed in high-risk locations, signs warn the public, rules limit who can view and keep recordings, and independent bodies check how they are used.

In conclusion, surveillance cameras are useful in high-risk places, but they should be used with clear rules and safeguards, because unrestricted surveillance would undermine privacy.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for digital wellbeing, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Many people say that they spend more time on their phones than they intend, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for digital wellbeing or whether society and government should take action. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that digital wellbeing depends on personal habits. Users can set limits on screen time, switch off notifications, keep phones out of bedrooms and make time for sport, friends and sleep. A person who leaves the phone in another room during meals, for example, enjoys the conversation more and sleeps better. Adults can teach children by example, and individuals who feel that a device is harming their mood can choose to use it less. Since people differ in how they react to technology, solutions suited to individual lives are more flexible than general rules, and personal choice respects freedom.

On the other hand, supporters of wider action point out that digital wellbeing is shaped by how products are designed. Many apps are built to hold attention for as long as possible, using endless scrolling, autoplay and notifications that exploit psychological weaknesses. A video app that starts the next clip automatically, for example, makes it easy to lose an hour without deciding to. Children, who are less able to resist, are especially vulnerable. Governments can require clear time-tracking tools, ban manipulative design aimed at children, set age limits and fund education about healthy use, and schools can teach digital skills. Companies also have a duty to avoid design that harms users.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility is shared: users should manage their habits, but companies and governments must stop products from exploiting people and must protect young users.

essays.question: Some believe that government surveillance is necessary for safety. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
After every serious attack, governments ask for greater powers to monitor communications, and some believe that government surveillance is necessary for safety. I agree only to a limited extent, since surveillance can prevent serious crime, but it threatens freedom when it is unchecked.

To begin with, surveillance can prevent serious crime and save lives. Monitoring communications and movements helps police to stop terrorism and organised crime, and technology allows them to find suspects far faster than in the past. Police who need a court order before reading a suspect's messages, for example, can investigate serious crime without spying on everyone. Intelligence work has foiled plots that would have caused many deaths, and surveillance of known networks of traffickers and fraudsters protects victims. Most citizens accept that targeted monitoring of dangerous individuals is a reasonable price for security.

However, mass collection invades privacy, can be misused against critics and may make citizens afraid to speak. Governments have sometimes used surveillance powers to monitor journalists, activists and political opponents, and large databases can be hacked or leaked. People who know that they are watched may avoid searching for sensitive information or joining legitimate protests, which weakens democracy. Evidence that bulk surveillance prevents more attacks than targeted methods is limited. Surveillance should therefore be limited by law: powers should be targeted, approved by courts, reviewed by independent bodies, and open to public reporting, and data should be deleted when no longer needed. These safeguards balance safety and liberty.

In conclusion, government surveillance is necessary for safety only to a limited extent, in targeted and supervised forms, and unrestricted surveillance poses a danger to the freedoms that it is meant to protect.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for preventing cybercrime, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Phishing emails, ransomware and online fraud cost people and businesses billions every year, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for preventing cybercrime or whether society and government should take action. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that careful behaviour prevents many attacks. People can update software regularly, use strong passwords, enable two-step verification and avoid clicking on unknown links or sharing codes. A person who ignores a software update, for example, may leave a gap that criminals use to steal data. Most attacks depend on human mistakes, such as replying to a fake message, so training and vigilance are the first line of defence. Parents can teach children about online risks, and employees who follow security rules protect their organisations. Individuals who take sensible precautions make themselves much harder targets.

On the other hand, advocates of action by society and government point out that criminals operate across borders and use methods that ordinary users cannot detect. Preventing cybercrime needs careful users, secure organisations and international law enforcement. Banks and companies must secure systems and report breaches, internet providers can block known malicious sites, and governments must pass laws, train specialist police and cooperate with other countries to pursue offenders. A person who is deceived by a highly convincing fake website, for instance, is the victim of professional criminals, not simply careless. Weak links at any level can undo the others.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that governments and organisations must take the main responsibility for security and enforcement, while individuals support them by taking sensible precautions.

essays.question: Many people think that online privacy is disappearing. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Every time we search for a product, use a map or accept a cookie, information about us is recorded, and many people think that online privacy is disappearing. I agree with this view, since almost every action leaves a data trail, although laws and tools can limit the loss.

To begin with, online privacy is shrinking because almost every action leaves a data trail. Websites, apps and devices track what people search, buy and where they go, companies sell the resulting profiles, and few users read the terms that they accept. A shopper who searches for a pair of shoes, for example, may see advertisements for them on a dozen unrelated websites. Smart speakers, fitness bands and connected televisions collect information inside the home, and cameras with facial recognition identify people in public. Data breaches expose the details of millions of people at once, so that information once shared can never be fully recovered.

Furthermore, privacy is also reduced by the habits of users, who often share photographs, locations and opinions freely on social media, and by governments that gather data for security purposes. Many people feel resigned, believing that they have nothing to hide or that avoiding services is impossible. However, privacy is not completely lost. Laws such as the European data protection rules give citizens rights to see, correct and delete their data and impose penalties for abuse. Individuals can use privacy settings, encrypted messaging, ad blockers and careful sharing to limit tracking. Privacy has not disappeared, but it now has to be actively defended through law, technology and personal choice.

In conclusion, I agree that online privacy is disappearing, because data are collected on an unprecedented scale, but laws and individual action can still slow the process.

essays.question: Many feel that online anonymity encourages bad behaviour. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
On many websites, people can post without using their real names, and many feel that online anonymity encourages bad behaviour. I agree to a large extent, since people who cannot be identified feel free to insult and harass others, although anonymity also protects people who need it.

To begin with, anonymity can encourage bad behaviour because it removes the fear of consequences. People who cannot be identified feel free to insult and harass others. A user with a false name who insults strangers, for example, behaves in a way that he would never dare to in person. Researchers call this the online disinhibition effect: without a face and a reputation, people may feel less empathy and more aggression. Trolling, hate speech, threats and the spread of false stories are more common where accounts are anonymous, and victims may find it very difficult to hold anyone responsible. Young people are especially vulnerable to anonymous bullying, which can continue day and night.

However, anonymity also has legitimate uses. Whistleblowers, victims of abuse and citizens in repressive states depend on it to speak safely, and many people use pseudonyms to discuss sensitive subjects such as health or sexuality without fear of judgement. Banning anonymity entirely would remove these protections and give platforms and governments great power over personal information. Moreover, real names do not always prevent abuse, since many people behave badly under their own names. A balanced approach is to allow pseudonyms but to require platforms to deal quickly with abuse, to enable police to identify serious offenders through proper legal procedures, and to give users tools to block and report harassment.

In conclusion, online anonymity encourages bad behaviour to a large extent, but it also protects people who need it, so rules should punish abuse without removing safe ways to speak.

essays.question: Some people believe that technology reduces face-to-face interaction. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
In cafes, trains and living rooms, people can be seen looking at screens instead of at one another, and opinions differ on whether technology reduces face-to-face interaction. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of this view argue that technology can reduce face-to-face contact. Time spent on screens can replace conversation, and people may prefer to text rather than meet. A family that scrolls through phones at dinner, for example, shares the same table but not the same conversation. Children who spend hours on games or videos may play less with friends, and workers who use messaging may avoid walking to a colleague's desk. Researchers have linked heavy social media use with loneliness, since online contact can feel less satisfying than real company. Habits such as checking phones during conversations also signal that the person present is less important than the device.

On the other hand, others point out that technology also helps people to meet. Messaging, video calls and social networks keep distant friends and relatives in touch, and people use apps to arrange gatherings, find groups with shared interests and organise events. Migrants and students living abroad can speak to their families every day. Online communities can reduce isolation for people with illnesses or unusual interests, who may not find others like them nearby. Many online friendships lead to meetings in person.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that the outcome depends on how technology is used: when devices replace personal contact, relationships suffer, but when they support it, they can strengthen links between people.

essays.question: Many people think that mobile apps have improved productivity. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Calendars, messaging tools, note-taking apps and project boards are now part of working life, and many people think that mobile apps have improved productivity. I agree with this view to a large extent, since apps save time by organising, automating and connecting work, although they can also distract.

To begin with, mobile apps save time by organising, automating and connecting work. Calendars, task lists, shared documents and messaging remove delays and paperwork. A team that uses a shared calendar and chat app, for example, can arrange a meeting in minutes instead of exchanging dozens of emails. Apps allow people to work from anywhere, reply to customers instantly and scan documents or sign contracts without printing. Scheduling tools, expense trackers and reminders reduce errors and forgotten tasks, and automation tools handle repetitive actions such as sending invoices. For small businesses and freelancers, affordable apps provide capabilities that once required an office and staff.

Furthermore, apps help individuals to manage their own time and learning. Fitness trackers, language lessons and budgeting tools encourage regular habits, and collaborative platforms allow colleagues in different countries to work together. However, productivity does not rise automatically. Notifications and endless features can distract and reduce real output, and constant availability may blur the line between work and rest, leading to stress. Research suggests that people check their phones many times a day and take time to refocus afterwards. Productivity improves when people choose a few tools, switch off unnecessary alerts and set times for deep work. Used with discipline, apps are a major help.

In conclusion, I agree that mobile apps have improved productivity to a large extent, because they save time and reduce effort, provided that users manage distractions carefully.

essays.question: How can governments ensure fair access to high-speed internet? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Fast internet has become as essential as electricity for study, work and public services, yet connection quality varies enormously between cities and countryside and between rich and poor households. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on building networks where the market will not and on keeping prices fair.

To begin with, governments should treat fast internet as essential infrastructure. Companies avoid sparsely populated areas because they are unprofitable, so public funding, shared networks, price regulation and low-cost plans are needed to bring fast service to rural and poorer households. A village that receives fast broadband, for example, allows a small business to sell its products online and children to study with the same tools as city pupils. Governments can pay for fibre cables to remote areas, offer grants or tax relief to firms that build there, and require operators to share masts and ducts, which lowers costs. Targets for coverage can be set in licences, with penalties for operators that fail to meet them.

In addition, authorities should keep services affordable and competitive. Regulation of prices, support for new providers and rules that prevent monopolies keep costs down, and social tariffs help low-income families. Public wifi in libraries, schools and community centres gives a basic level of access for those who cannot afford a home connection. A universal service obligation, which guarantees every household a minimum speed at a reasonable price, ensures that nobody is left behind. Equally important, public services and schools should plan for people with poor connections. These measures cost money, but economic growth, education and access to services in underserved regions more than repay it.

In conclusion, investing in networks where the market will not and regulating prices and competition offer the most realistic way of ensuring fair access to high-speed internet.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that electric vehicles should be subsidized?

versions.text:
Sales of electric cars are rising, but they are still more expensive than petrol models, and many governments offer money to buyers. I agree to a large extent that electric vehicles should be subsidised, provided that the support is temporary and well targeted.

To begin with, subsidies are justified because they speed up the shift to cleaner transport. Buyers face high prices and a lack of chargers, so support speeds up adoption and cuts emissions. A family on a modest income, for example, may only buy an electric car if a grant lowers its price. As more cars are sold, factories can produce at a larger scale and batteries become cheaper, which eventually removes the need for help. Transport is a major source of greenhouse gases and local air pollution, so that early adoption brings benefits to public health as well as to the climate. Subsidies also encourage manufacturers and investors to build charging networks.

However, unlimited subsidies have drawbacks. Grants mostly benefit wealthy households that would have bought an electric car anyway, and they cost public money that could improve public transport, which helps everyone, including people without cars. Support should therefore be time-limited, based on income and linked to investment in charging points, and it should decrease as prices fall. Some countries have already ended or reduced grants once sales were established. Governments may also need to ensure that electricity is produced from clean sources, otherwise the environmental benefit will be limited.

In conclusion, I agree that electric vehicles should be subsidised, but only in a temporary, targeted way that is combined with charging infrastructure.

essays.question: How far do you think autonomous delivery robots will become common in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Small wheeled robots that carry parcels and meals along pavements are already used in a few cities, and the question is how common they will become within twenty years. I believe that they will become common in suitable areas, but not everywhere.

To begin with, delivery robots have clear advantages that will encourage their spread. They cut labour costs and emissions on short trips, and they can work at night and deliver quickly. A small robot that brings lunch to students across a university campus, for example, works well on wide, quiet paths. As online shopping and food delivery grow, companies will look for cheaper ways to complete the final stage of a journey, which is the most expensive part. Improvements in sensors and artificial intelligence will help robots to avoid obstacles and cross roads safely, and falling hardware prices will make large fleets affordable.

However, several obstacles will limit where they can operate. Crowded pavements, kerbs, stairs and bad weather make movement difficult, especially in old and dense city centres. Theft, vandalism and public concern about safety could provoke restrictive rules, and many people feel uneasy about machines sharing the pavement with children and the elderly. They also threaten jobs for couriers, which may cause political opposition. Use will therefore grow in campuses, new suburbs and business parks, where space and infrastructure suit robots, rather than in the centres of old cities. For large or heavy items, drones and vans will remain more practical.

In conclusion, delivery robots will become common in suitable areas within twenty years, but they will not replace human couriers across entire cities.

essays.question: How far do you think quantum computing will affect industry in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Quantum computers use the strange behaviour of particles to carry out certain calculations, and the question is how far they will affect industry within twenty years. I believe that they will transform a few industries, although they will remain specialised tools.

To begin with, quantum computers will change fields that depend on very complex calculations. They can simulate molecules and solve some optimisation problems far faster than ordinary machines, helping drug and materials research. A drug company that can simulate how a molecule behaves, for example, may find a new medicine in months instead of years. Airlines, shipping firms and energy companies could also use them to plan routes and manage networks more efficiently, saving fuel and money. In finance, quantum methods may improve the assessment of risk, and governments are already preparing new forms of encryption because these machines could break current codes.

However, the effect on industry as a whole is likely to be limited. Errors are common, the machines are extremely expensive and need extreme cooling, and only a small number of problems benefit from quantum methods. Most businesses need computers for ordinary tasks such as accounting, communication and design, for which existing machines are perfectly adequate. Experts disagree about how soon practical devices will appear, and companies may have to pay to access them through the cloud instead of owning them. Wider effects within twenty years are therefore likely to be limited to specialist fields.

In conclusion, quantum computing will affect a few industries deeply over the next twenty years, but it is unlikely to change industry as a whole.

essays.question: Do the advantages of space exploration outweigh its high cost? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
A single space mission can cost more than the annual budget of a small country, and the question is whether the advantages of space exploration outweigh its high cost. This essay will discuss both sides before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, space exploration drives technology and knowledge that benefit people on Earth. Satellites provide weather forecasts, navigation, communication and climate data, and techniques developed for space, such as lightweight materials and medical monitors, have found uses in daily life. A farmer who receives a satellite weather forecast, for example, can decide when to plant and avoid losing a crop. Space science also inspires students, creates skilled jobs and encourages international cooperation, as seen in joint research stations. Discoveries about other planets improve our understanding of climate and of the conditions that make life possible.

On the negative side, space programmes cost enormous sums that could address urgent problems on Earth. Missions run to billions, with uncertain returns, while hospitals, schools and housing lack funds, and failures waste money and sometimes lives. The sum spent on a single mission, for example, could equip dozens of hospitals in poorer regions. Many of the most useful applications are already established, so that further crewed missions to distant places add little practical benefit. Moreover, rocket launches create pollution and increase the amount of debris around the planet.

In conclusion, the practical and scientific benefits are considerable, but costs must be controlled. On balance, I believe that the advantages outweigh the cost when spending focuses on useful programmes such as satellites and climate monitoring, rather than on prestige projects.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using biometric ID systems.

versions.text:
Fingerprint scanners on phones, face recognition at airports and iris checks at banks have made biometric identification part of everyday life, and many governments plan national systems. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using biometric ID systems before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, biometric identification is secure and convenient. Fingerprints and faces are hard to forge, and they speed up checks at borders and banks. A traveller who passes an automatic border gate with a fingerprint scan, for example, saves time but leaves personal data in a government database. Biometric systems reduce identity fraud, since a stolen password or card is useless without the matching body feature, and they are convenient because users have nothing to remember or carry. In poorer countries, national biometric IDs have enabled millions of people without documents to access banking, welfare and voting for the first time.

On the negative side, biometric systems carry lasting privacy risks. A stolen fingerprint cannot be changed in the way a password can, databases attract hackers, and errors can wrongly exclude people, particularly those with worn fingerprints or darker skin when software is poorly trained. Governments or companies could use the data to track people or share it without consent. Some individuals may be unable to use the system at all and risk losing access to services. Nevertheless, these concerns can be reduced through strong encryption, strict laws on how biometric data may be stored and shared, independent audits, and fair alternatives for those who cannot or will not use biometrics.

In conclusion, biometric ID systems offer security and convenience, but the risks to privacy and fairness are serious. On balance, I believe that they should be adopted only where there is strong data protection and reliable alternatives.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on digital infrastructure or on traditional infrastructure? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Governments are asked to build fast networks for a digital economy, but roads, bridges, power lines and water pipes also need money, and opinions differ on which kind of infrastructure should receive priority. This essay will discuss both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of digital infrastructure argue that it drives growth. Fast internet supports remote work, online services and business growth, and it gives access to education and healthcare in remote areas. A village that receives fast broadband, for example, allows a small business to sell its products online and children to study with the same tools as city pupils. Digital networks also make government services cheaper and faster, and countries with good connections attract investment in modern industries. Since more and more of daily life takes place online, those without connections are left behind.

On the other hand, supporters of traditional infrastructure argue that it is the foundation of everyday life. Digital networks depend on traditional infrastructure, so spending should balance the two. Broadband needs reliable electricity, roads and water to function, and neglected basic infrastructure harms everyday life and safety through accidents, floods and power cuts. A town with fast broadband but frequent power cuts, for example, still cannot support online businesses. Bridges and railways also move goods and people, which no network can replace.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that governments should divide spending according to each region's biggest gap, since priority should depend on need, and that traditional infrastructure should not be neglected.

essays.question: Discuss how citizen science projects can benefit research.

versions.text:
Citizen science projects invite ordinary people to help scientists by counting wildlife, recording the weather or classifying images, and they are growing in many countries. This essay will discuss how these projects can benefit research, focusing on the quantity of data and on the involvement of the public.

To begin with, citizen science benefits research by supplying large amounts of data at low cost. Thousands of volunteers can record observations over wide areas and long periods that scientists could not cover. Thousands of volunteers who record the birds in their gardens, for example, give scientists a picture of population changes that no small team could collect. Such data can show how species move as the climate changes, or how pollution varies from place to place. Because volunteers are not paid, projects can continue for many years, and they allow researchers to spend their limited funds on analysis instead of collection. Online platforms in which volunteers classify galaxies or photographs have also led to real discoveries.

Furthermore, taking part builds public understanding and trust. Volunteers learn how science works, become more interested in the subject and are more likely to support research funding and to change their own behaviour, for example by protecting local habitats. Students who join projects gain practical skills, and communities feel that their knowledge is valued. However, quality can vary, so training, clear instructions and checks by experts are needed to keep data reliable. When well organised, citizen science makes research broader, cheaper and more trusted.

In conclusion, citizen science benefits research by providing large quantities of data and engaging the public, provided that quality is carefully controlled.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of mass digitization of public records.

versions.text:
Birth certificates, land registers, court files and archives are being scanned and moved online in many countries, and the question is whether mass digitisation of public records is wise. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, digitising public records makes them easier to find and preserve. Citizens can search archives and obtain documents online, paper is saved and fragile records are protected from fire, damp and decay. A citizen who orders a birth certificate online, for example, avoids a journey to a distant office. Digital records can be copied and stored in several places, which protects against loss, and they can be searched in seconds instead of hours. Governments can save money on storage and staff, reduce errors and corruption by making changes traceable, and share information between departments to offer faster services. Historians and researchers also gain access to material that was once available only to those who could visit an archive.

On the negative side, digitisation creates new risks. Large databases attract hackers, and a single breach can expose the personal details of millions of people. People without internet access or digital skills, often older or poorer citizens, may be excluded from services that are available only online. The cost of conversion, security and maintenance can be high, and formats and software become obsolete, so records may become unreadable in the future. Nevertheless, these problems can be managed through strong security, regular backups, clear rules on access to sensitive data, continued offline options for those who need them and open standards.

In conclusion, mass digitisation of public records brings substantial benefits, but it requires strong protection and fair access. On balance, I believe that it is worthwhile, provided that security and inclusion are taken seriously.

analysis.type_vi: A/D: số hoá hàng loạt hồ sơ công

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hiện tượng (giấy khai sinh, sổ đăng ký đất, hồ sơ toà án, kho lưu trữ đang được quét và đưa lên mạng); kết luận có điều kiện (an ninh và hòa nhập).

Dễ tìm và bảo quản: công dân tìm kiếm, lấy tài liệu trực tuyến; tiết kiệm giấy, bảo vệ hồ sơ mong manh khỏi lửa, ẩm, mục. Ví dụ công dân đặt giấy khai sinh trực tuyến tránh đi xa đến văn phòng. Bản số sao chép lưu nhiều nơi; tìm trong vài giây thay vì hàng giờ; chính phủ tiết kiệm lưu trữ, nhân viên, giảm sai sót và tham nhũng nhờ thay đổi truy vết được; chia sẻ giữa các bộ phận; nhà sử học tiếp cận tài liệu trước đây chỉ người đến kho mới xem.

Rủi ro mới: cơ sở dữ liệu lớn thu hút tin tặc, một vụ rò rỉ lộ thông tin hàng triệu người; người không có internet hoặc kỹ năng số (già, nghèo) có thể bị loại khỏi dịch vụ chỉ có trực tuyến; chi phí chuyển đổi, an ninh, bảo trì cao; định dạng và phần mềm lỗi thời nên hồ sơ có thể không đọc được. Nevertheless: an ninh mạnh, sao lưu thường xuyên, quy tắc rõ truy cập dữ liệu nhạy cảm, giữ lựa chọn ngoại tuyến, chuẩn mở.
Đáng làm nếu an ninh và hoà nhập được coi trọng.
